Kaboré, to appear'); published as Corela 7(1), 2009, doi:10.4000/corela.134. Corroboration: Alerechi, Roseline Ihuoma C. 2020. The syllable structure of Ikwere. ERUDITE Journal of Linguistics and Language 2(1): 82-103, p. 91.
catalog_locator: Preprint pp. 14-16, section 3.2 (word-final m; tone schemes of disyllabic nouns, examples (16) and the two paragraphs below them). Alerechi 2020 corroboration: journal p. 91.
catalog_quote: pourquoi le m en position finale de mot porte un ton, alors que, normalement, seules les voyelles (y compris bien évidemment la nasale moraïque) portent un ton. [...] La première colonne montre que chaque nom dissyllabique présente un de sept schèmes tonals. Il s’agit de toutes les combinaisons possibles de H et B soumises aux quatre contraintes suivantes: 1) les noms ne portent pas de ton montant (BH), 2) les tons descendants (HB) apparaissent seulement sur la syllabe finale, 3) les tons H abaissés n'apparaissent que sur la syllabe finale et seulement après un ton H, et 4) aucune syllabe ne porte plus de deux tons. [...] Enfin, la première colonne montre également que les syllabes finales en ikwere présentent seulement quatre schèmes contrastifs: H, B, descendant (HB) et montant (BH). [Alerechi 2020: 91: The peak of every syllable in Ikwere bears a tone. Thus tone is the determinant factor for identifying a syllable in the language.]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.translation: normally only vowels (including, of course, the moraic nasal) bear a tone. [...] The first column shows that each disyllabic noun displays one of seven tone schemes. These are all the possible combinations of H and L subject to the following four constraints: 1) nouns do not bear a rising tone (LH), 2) falling tones (HL) appear only on the final syllable, 3) downstepped H tones appear only on the final syllable and only after an H tone, and 4) no syllable bears more than two tones.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (18 pp., text; = extracted text). Both parts of the quote are present verbatim: p. 14 (end of section 3.2 argument against a phonemic /m/): "pourquoi le m en position finale de mot porte un ton, alors que, normalement, seules les voyelles (y compris bien évidemment la nasale moraïque) portent un ton."; p. 15, below table (16): "La première colonne montre que chaque nom dissyllabique présente un de sept schèmes tonals. Il s'agit de toutes les combinaisons possibles de H et B soumises aux quatre contraintes suivantes : 1) les noms ne portent pas de ton montant (BH), 2) les tons descendants (HB) apparaissent seulement sur la syllabe finale, 3) les tons H abaissés n'apparaissent que sur…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikwere is a register-tone language: every syllable peak (vowel or moraic nasal) carries lexical tone (H, L, downstepped H, with HL/LH contours restricted to final syllables); disyllabic nouns fall into seven tone schemes (Alerechi 2020 p. 87: eight noun tone classes, 4-8 per dialect). No opened source says anything about word stress or accent; there is no statement of stress placement, and none saying explicitly that stress is absent.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress. Tonal: rising tone absent from nouns but present on a few verbs (Alerechi 2020 pp. 92-93); Clark 1971 also records 'Mid' tones in Ikwere list items (High High Mid), a mid level not used by Osu & Clements.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: disyllabic nouns in isolation and CVm words, Ogbakiri dialect (first author's own speech). Corroborated by Alerechi 2020 p. 91 (Omuanwa/Ogbakiri): 'The peak of every syllable in Ikwere bears a tone.'
new_statements.identity_note: Osu & Clements describe the Ogbakiri dialect (Glottolog ogba1242, first author's own speech); Alerechi's data are Omuanwa (omua?; not in Glottolog's 18 dialects) and Ogbakiri; Alerechi 2020 counts 24 mutually intelligible dialects with 4-8 noun tone classes each. All sources treat Ikwere as one language (ISO ikw), distinct from Igbo.

tone_statements.citation: Alerechi, Roseline Ihuoma C. n.d. [c. 2018-2020]. Some linguistic features of the Ikwere language. International Journal of Advancement in Education, Management, Science and Technology 3(1): 108-123.
tone_statements.quote: Williamson (1980), Worukwo (1983), Alerechi (1987) and Azunda (1987) identify five tones in the language. The five tones consist of two basic tones, low ( `) and high (´ ) tones; a downstep represented here as ( ̄), and two contour tones - falling ( ̂ ) and rising ( ̌ ) tones. [...] In Ikwere, the floating tone causes the lowering of the following high tone. On the other hand, the falling and rising tones can be analyzed as a combination of high and low (HL) and low and high (LH) tones, respectively. Rising tone is rare in some of the dialects of Ikwere. [...] Tone, therefore, performs lexical and grammatical functions in the language.
tone_statements.n_tones: 5: 2 level (H, L) + downstepped H + 2 contour (HL falling, LH rising)

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Ogbakiri dialect (first author's own). Tones: H, B(=L), downstepped H; disyllabic nouns show seven tone schemes built from H and L under four constraints (no rising tone on nouns, HL and downstepped H only on the final syllable, max two tones per syllable); 'normalement, seules les voyelles (y compris.. la nasale moraïque) portent un ton' (preprint p. 14-15). Published Corela version checked online: same constraints at paragraph 62.

sources.citation: Clements, G. N. & Sylvester Osu. 2003. Ikwere nasal harmony in typological perspective. In P. Sauzet & A. Zribi-Hertz (eds.), Typologie des langues d'Afrique et universaux de la grammaire, vol. II. Paris: L'Harmattan.
sources.note: No statement on Ikwere stress. Segmental sketch (vowels, ATR harmony, oral/nasal contrasts) with tone-marked examples; mentions 'a placeless, tone-bearing nasal vowel' (p. 4). The only 'accentual' remark (p. 18-19) is cross-linguistic: nonexplosive stops 'never bear tonal or accentual features'.

sources.citation: Alerechi, Roseline Ihuoma C. n.d. [c. 2018-2020]. Some linguistic features of the Ikwere language. International Journal of Advancement in Education, Management, Science and Technology 3(1): 108-123.
sources.quote: Williamson (1980), Worukwo (1983), Alerechi (1987) and Azunda (1987) identify five tones in the language. The five tones consist of two basic tones, low ( `) and high (´ ) tones; a downstep represented here as ( ̄), and two contour tones - falling ( ̂ ) and rising ( ̌ ) tones. [...] In Ikwere, the floating tone causes the lowering of the following high tone. On the other hand, the falling and rising tones can be analyzed as a combination of high and low (HL) and low and high (LH) tones, respectively. Rising tone is rare in some of the dialects of Ikwere. [...] Tone, therefore, performs lexical and grammatical functions in the language.
sources.note: First-hand overview with a dedicated 'Tones' section: five tones = two level tones (low, high), a downstep (a floating tone lowers a following high), and two contour tones, falling (=HL) and rising (=LH), the rising tone rare in some dialects; tone has lexical and grammatical (e.g. negation) function; disyllabic nouns fall into eight tone classes (four to eight depending on dialect); monosyllabic verbs into three tone classes; every syllable peak (vowel or syllabic nasal) carries a tone; verb inflection partly marked by tonal modification.
